Skip next section Far-right politicians call for migrant expulsions, security reinforcement 08/02/2026 August 2, 2026 Far-right politicians call for migrant expulsions, security reinforcement Abascal called for the border with Morocco to be closed immediately Image: Gabriela Sardá Núñez/Europa Press/IMAGO The border crisis in Ceuta has sparked debates in Spain and across Europe about the Spanish government's migration policy. Many governments in Europe have sought to curb immigration, but Spain has pursued a different approach, recently announcing a plan to provide legal status to up to 500,000 undocumented migrants. Pedro Sanchez and his Socialist government have been heavily criticized this week by politicians from Spain's right and far-right parties. The leader of the opposition, the conservative People's Party's Alberto Nunez Feijoo, has traveled to the exclave, where he slammed Sanchez for failing to prevent the border rush. The leader of the far-right Vox party, Santiago Abascal, who was also in Ceuta on Sunday, blamed the Socialist government for the migrant surge, which he described as "an invasion." He said the surge was an "act of war" and an "attack on the sovereignty and security of Spaniards." Abascal also said Sanchez was "a danger" to the country, and called for the EU-Morocco agreement, which functions as a partial free trade area, to be scrapped. Far-right influencer and Member of the European Parliament Alvise Perez called for migrants to be expelled during a confrontation with a crowd of rival protesters in Ceuta. Much of the city's population is of Moroccan descent. Perez had to shelter in a bar before being escorted away by police. Sanchez and his government have also been criticized by other right-wing politicians in Europe, most notably Italy's Interior Minister Antonio Tajani. Italy has suspended free movement with Spain, even though both are part of the Schengen Area. https://p.dw.com/p/5I9jz Skip next section Most migrants return but Ceuta still on edge as death toll climbs to 72 08/02/2026 August 2, 2026 Most migrants return but Ceuta still on edge as death toll climbs to 72 Karl Sexton | Jenipher Camino Gonzalez Editor Between 50,000 and 60,000 mostly male migrants broke into Ceuta this week Image: Henry Nicholls/AFP Relative calm had returned to Ceuta on Sunday, but the city remained on edge following the deadly border rush. Local officials have warned that the city's recovery has just begun, while right-wing politicians are blaming the Socialist government in Madrid for chaotic scenes that unfolded this week in the Spanish North African exclave. Spanish Civil Guard ships were searching the waters around the city on Sunday for more bodies after between 50,000 and 60,000 migrants breached the border with Morocco. Nearly all of them had walked back to the Moroccan side of the border by Sunday, according to officials in Ceuta, normally home to around 84,000 people. At least 72 people died during the crush on Thursday and Friday, the Spanish government representative in Ceuta, Miguel Angel Perez, said. Some drowned, while others were killed in a stampede at a breakwater barrier and a border fence. Perez added that medical services have treated more than 1,000 people. He said while the situation in the exclave had improved significantly, work remained to be done for the city to return to normal. On Saturday, authorities installed a 500-meter (1,600-foot) floating barrier in the waters off Ceuta to boost border security, as well as reinforcing police and army patrols. https://www.dw.com/en/water-conflict-aro.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5J4xl Once considered a water-rich state, Brandenburg is now facing challenges on several fronts Image: Patrick Pleul/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement For years, Petra Liesenfeld has witnessed falling groundwater levels in her hometown of Baruth. She has to water her garden far more often than she used to, and has seen some local trees completely dry out. At the same time, two beverage companies are looking to expand production in the area. Mineral water has been bottled in the small town of Baruth, which lies around 60 kilometers (37 miles) south of Berlin, since the 1990s. The site is now run by Red Bull and Austrian beverage producer Rauch, who are planning a new canning factory and additional facilities. All in the middle of a water protection area. The Baruth waterworks are licensed to extract a fixed amount of groundwater each year, just 8% of which goes to supply the town's roughly 4,300 residents with drinking water. The remaining 92% is reserved for Red Bull and Rauch, and is enough to cover the drinking water needs of 57,000 people. But exactly how much water the companies currently use is not made public. How much Red Bull and Rauch pay for the daily 7 million liters of permitted groundwater is confidential Image: DW This is legal under the existing contracts, said Peter Ilk, who until recently was the town's mayor and is considered a driving force behind the region's industrialization. He sees no problem with the way water is managed. "We have always given priority to supplying the population. That is also written into all the contracts," he said, adding that it stands to reason that the companies need more than the town's residents. "That's how you end up with this ratio of around one to 10 in terms of consumption." Old data informing current decisions Hydrogeologist Irina Engelhardt from the Technical University in Berlin takes a more critical view, pointing out that the contracts, which are around 30 years old, are based on outdated information. Since then, groundwater levels, groundwater recharge and the way land is used have all changed significantly. "I am concerned at how the water situation is developing in the state of Brandenburg," she said. "The volume that is actually available is currently being overestimated by the Brandenburg authorities." Members of the local initiative reached out to the authorities to get an idea of the situation, but many of the documents they received had been heavily redacted Image: DW Together with a citizens' initiative made up of local residents, she is calling for new, independent assessments — and for clear and open communication. Though the authorities granted them access to some groundwater monitoring documents, large parts were redacted, which some residents believe is a move to conceal information about changes in levels. "We ask ourselves why there can't be more transparency if everything is aboveboard. Why isn't the public allowed to know?" said Petra Liesenfeld. Exactly how much Red Bull and Rauch pay for their daily extraction of up to 7 million liters of groundwater is not public information. DW approached both companies for comment, but by the time of publication, neither had responded. For drought researcher Andreas Marx, this lack of transparency is problematic. "By law, water is a public commodity. It cannot be privately owned. So, in my view, every decision made and every contract signed over its use should be open to the public," he said. How dry is Brandenburg? Germany — and Brandenburg — are still water-rich regions. Marx, who heads the Drought Monitor at the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research, said "the challenge isn't adapting to permanent water scarcity but learning how to cope with dry periods that can last two or even three years." Nevertheless, the water balance in the state, as elsewhere in Germany, is definitely changing. Since the 2018 drought, groundwater has not been sufficiently replenished in many places and higher temperatures and increasing evaporation are making it harder for reserves in deeper soil layers to recover. This could cause even more problems in the future, as 95% of Brandenburg's drinking water comes from groundwater. How much water does the energy transition need? In Grünheide, in the eastern part of the state of Brandenburg, Tesla's Gigafactory has a permit to extract up to 1.4 million cubic meters of water per year and is planning to expand production to as many as 7,500 vehicles per week. Meanwhile, in recent years, residents have repeatedly been urged to save water. Since the construction of Tesla's Gigafactory was announced in 2019, the project has faced strong criticism from local residents Image: DW "Many projects, including new schools and kindergartens, were put on hold because there simply wasn't enough water," said local resident Manu Hoyer. Andreas Marx says when water resources are scarce, residents are generally the first to face restrictions because they're the easiest to limit. "Industrial companies are rarely restricted, because the economic consequences are much harder to assess," he said. Copper for the energy transition – a risk to groundwater? The potential for an additional water problem is brewing further south in Spremberg, where a large mine is planned. Over the coming decades, copper — which is essential for power grids, electric vehicles , and the transition to clean energy — is set to be extracted from depths of up to 1,200 meters. Lignite mining has a long history in parts of Brandenburg Image: DW Geotechnical engineer Michael Pfeiffer says mine water from such depths is highly saline and sulphureous and requires extensive treatment. "But the treatment plant proposed so far is nowhere near capable of doing what's actually required to clean the water to a standard where it could be safely discharged into the Spree," Pfeiffer said of the river that flows north towards Berlin. The river's water is already affected by decades of lignite mining in the region, and it is facing additional pressures. With lignite extraction set to end by 2038 , the groundwater currently pumped into the Spree from the mines will no longer be available. As a result, dry summers could see the river carrying up to 75% less water, with far-reaching consequences for water resources all the way to Berlin. The race for water One possible solution to the water problems facing the state around the German capital is artificial groundwater recharge , where excess water from periods of high rainfall is stored underground and used later. In these basins in Brandenburg, treated wastewater is already deliberately allowed to seep into the ground, storing it for dry periods Image: DW Hydrogeologist Irina Engelhardt is researching where this could be possible in the region. "There are areas in Brandenburg — such as where Tesla is now located — where artificial groundwater recharge could meet almost the entire demand of the local drinking water supplier," she said. Though enough available water is necessary for this solution to work. For drought researcher Andreas Marx, one question remains crucial: What rules should determine how water is distributed between the population, agriculture, nature and industry during prolonged dry periods. As the global temperature continues to rise, it is an issue not reserved for Brandenburg — or even Germany. This article was originally published in German. The Tate brothers were arrested in Miami in late July after Britain requested their extradition. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Reuters Comments Share Save for later Please log in to bookmark this story. Log In Create Free Account Romanian prosecutors officially indicted social media influencer Andrew Tate on Friday for trafficking minors, money laundering, sex with a minor and witness tampering and his brother Tristan for complicity, years after they began investigating them. The Tate brothers, former kickboxers with dual U.S. and British citizenship, were arrested in Miami in late July after Britain requested their extradition. Mainly based in Romania since 2017, they have been under criminal investigation in the country on charges including human trafficking since December, 2022. Romanian prosecutors said the Tates recruited their victims by seducing them and falsely claiming to want a relationship or marriage, before forcing them to produce pornographic content for a webcam business. They have denied all wrongdoing. “We will examine every aspect of [the indictment] with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process,” a Romanian lawyer for the Tates, Eugen Vidineac, said in a statement. “Our clients continue to reject the allegations against them.” Tate brothers remain in Miami jail after U.S. judge declines to rule immediately on request for bail The Tate brothers remain in jail in the U.S. while a judge decides on the request for their extradition to Britain, where they are wanted on rape charges. The spokesperson for the Romanian anti-organized crime prosecuting unit DIICOT – which is investigating the Tates – said it was not immediately clear whether the unit will seek their extradition from the United States. The Tates can be tried in absentia in Romania, but the trial will not start immediately. Under Romanian law, the indictment gets sent to a preliminary court chamber, where a judge will inspect the case files to ensure legality. While the law states that the preliminary chamber judge has 60 days to finalize the report, indictments routinely take significantly longer. DIICOT said one of Andrew Tate’s victims was 15 when he seduced her in Britain in 2012, before moving her to the Romanian capital Bucharest and using physical violence and mental intimidation to sexually exploit her by forcing her to produce pornographic content for social media sites. His brother Tristan was an accessory, the unit said, using physical aggression to coerce the victim. Prosecutors said the brothers kept US$1.25-million from the videochat income generated by the victim, roughly 80 per cent of all her gains. The brothers tried to launder the funds by buying four luxury cars, they added. The brothers were previously indicted in Romania on charges of human trafficking, but in late 2024 the Bucharest court of appeals sent the case back to prosecutors after deeming some evidence inadmissible. Andrew Tate, a self-described misogynist, previously said he moved to Romania because law enforcement there was more lax. Both brothers have grown their following of mainly young men by building a lavish, hyper-macho image of driving fast cars and dating beautiful women. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmp3.text: Image source, Telewizja Polska SA By Alys Davies Â and Â Paul Adams ,Â Diplomatic correspondent ,Â Reporting from Kyiv Published 24 September 2026, 12:16 BST Updated 14 minutes ago A fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland was a deliberate "act of sabotage", a government minister has said. Polish Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said the fire in the Masovian Voivodeship province was "deliberately designed to disable the station... disrupting internet access for various institutions, including the Ukrainian army". He told Polish public broadcaster TVP Info an investigation was ongoing but "many indications suggest" the attack fits into a "new Russian doctrine of attack". The Kremlin has not commented. Meanwhile, Denmark's intelligence service issued a new threat assessment saying it expects Russia to escalate hybrid warfare in the coming months. It said an attack remained "highly unlikely" but warned of "a low but growing risk" that Russia could launch a limited military attack against Nato countries. In recent weeks a number of European Nato members have said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine, which Moscow denies. Earlier this month, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport , while France has ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites. Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary - for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation. Proxies are often used to carry out the attacks and Russia always denies involvement, despite growing evidence to the contrary. Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage - and Russia is the chief suspect Published 4 September The fire at the state-owned Polish satellite station broke out on Wednesday night in Wola Krobowska. It remains operational. The deputy prime minister said it transmits internet traffic through Poland to countries including Ukraine, and uses SpaceX systems that provide connectivity via Starlink terminals. Asked about the incident at a news conference with Bulgaria's leader on Thursday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he disliked "labelling something as sabotage versus an accident without 100% certainty, but it looks bad". Also on Thursday, Moldova's president said four Russian drones crossed into its airspace, with at least one exploding, while Romania's defence ministry said one drone crashed in its territory. On Wednesday Poland also said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace , forcing it to scramble fighter jets. Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Moscow does not plan to attack Nato states. Earlier this month, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said it was Europe speaking about preparing for war, adding: "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war [from that in Ukraine], and it will be very short." Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including the Crimea peninsula annexed in 2014. Ukraine is now experiencing round-the-clock attacks and near constant alerts. In Kharkiv, six people were killed and 12 others injured in a Russian strike on a farm in the village of Stara Hnylytsia, Ukraine's state emergency services said. It said they were agricultural workers sorting vegetables, with the head of the Kharkiv region adding that four were women. Image source, DSNS Ukraine Image caption, Onions covered the floor where the six farm workers were killed in Kharkiv In Kyiv, there were multiple explosions on Wednesday night as drones, ballistic and cruise missiles landed or were intercepted over the city. In the past 24 hours, a bakery, a pharmaceutical plant and a jewellery workshop were all hit. Strikes on several data centres also caused internet disruptions in areas of the city. Two people were killed and eight others injured overnight, emergency services said. One was killed when fragments of a drone landed close to a maternity hospital. The hospital's director said a woman gave birth to a baby boy in a shelter during that attack, adding: "Even on such a terrible night, life goes on." Russia's defence ministry said it had hit Ukrainian defence facilities, logistics and telecom centres, as well as vessels used by the military. Figure caption, Watch: Ukraine's race to counter a new type of Russian drone Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who is in New York for the UN General Assembly, accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. But it is sometimes hard to distinguish between deliberate and accidental hits. Attacks on power facilities, railways and data centres are all clearly part of a deliberate Russian strategy to make life as difficult as possible for civilians far from the slow-moving front lines. With its long-range attacks on oil refineries and postal warehouses, Ukraine is doing something similar: bringing the war home to ordinary Russians. But Russia's attacks on Ukraine's cities have intensified in recent weeks. Jet-powered drones are now more common than their slower predecessors, which used piston engines. The latest Russian drones fly high and fast, making them harder to shoot down. There's also less time for civilians to react. Kyiv is racing to develop low-cost weapons that can counter them as the missiles and fighter jets it has to fight back are too expensive. In New York, Zelensky said, "we need ballistic interceptors to protect lives" and called on the US to help. He said Putin needed to be stopped from continuing the war and "spreading this evil further", adding: "Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land." The Ukrainian president's comments came as Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev headed to the US to meet Trump administration officials, including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Reuters reported, citing two sources. Russia's Lavrov told the UN Security Council on Wednesday there would be no pause in the war. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: A premature baby in an incubator in a hospital in Zaporizhzhia. Organisations in Ukraine report an anecdotal rise in maternal and child mortalities. Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP View image in fullscreen A premature baby in an incubator in a hospital in Zaporizhzhia. Organisations in Ukraine report an anecdotal rise in maternal and child mortalities. Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP Ukraine in depth World news ‘The nurse used the torch on her phone to do the op’: hospitals stripped of resources in Ukraine’s occupied territories Clinics and hospitals in affected areas lack staff, power and medicines, with supplies redirected to the Russian military Supported by About this content Ruchi Kumar Wed 7 Oct 2026 04.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 08.06 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google E arlier this summer, the once bustling corridors of the district hospital in Hola Prystan, a city in the Russian-occupied Kherson region of Ukraine , were ominously quiet. At times, it was plunged into darkness during power cuts lasting hours. Much of the hospital’s medical equipment and supplies had been stolen and redirected to the military, and many experienced staff had gone. “They [the Russian forces] even took some of the furniture,” says Natalia Sergeevna, who spent more than two decades working as a nurse in the hospital before escaping to Ukrainian-held territory in July. In some ways, her hospital had been lucky, she says, with others in Russian-occupied territories repurposed for military use – as has been happening in regions bordering Ukraine – or simply closed down. Despite its bare-bones infrastructure and dark corridors, people still came to the hospital, says Sergeevna, often making difficult journeys across the mine-infested landscape of occupied Kherson. View image in fullscreen A hospital damaged by Russian shelling in Kherson in July. Photograph: Global Images Ukraine/Getty Images “They came with injuries and wounds; they came looking for oncologists or endocrinologists or palliative care. Women still came with pregnancies,” she says, “but every day it was getting harder to help them.” In recent months, the situation has deteriorated further, with blockades and supply shortages leaving some Russian-occupied territories with limited medical support. In June, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said conditions in Oleshky and Hola Prystan , where Sergeevna worked, were becoming desperate, with thousands of people left without food, water and medicines. It said ambulances had stopped coming to people’s homes, with medical assistance only available for the most urgent cases and patients dying during attempted evacuations. Sergeevna says she had stayed in the hope of liberation, but by the summer things had become unbearable. “There is almost no available support to do any kind of surgeries; even basic procedures like removing polyps aren’t possible. View image in fullscreen A woman takes care of a baby in a shelter in the city of Sievierodonetsk, Donbas region. Photograph: Fadel Senna/AFP/Getty Images “In one case this year, we were performing a C-section, and the woman developed uterine bleeding, but there was no blood available for transfusion, because all of the supplies had been sent to the [Russian] soldiers,” she says. Another obstacle is the forced “passportisation ” of the population in occupied territories, with medical services refused to people who do not have a Russian compulsory health insurance policy, which can only be obtained through a Russian passport. “They treat you very badly if you are Ukrainian. We have no rights, they tell us to our face, ‘you’re a nobody’,” says Marina*, who lives in a town occupied by Russian forces. She says she had to be taken to hospital in 2023 after she developed complications during her pregnancy and went into early labour. “The baby was coming with the backside down, and I needed an emergency C-section. I was in a lot of pain,” she says. “But it was 11.30pm, and the curfew was in place. We tried getting out, but they shot at us.” View image in fullscreen A member of an emergency medical aid team working in Kherson. Photograph: Global Images Ukraine/Getty Images Marina says she spent an excruciating night cared for by her husband and a neighbour, before rushing to the clinic as soon as the curfew lifted. “When we got there, there was no obstetrician, no qualified staff for pregnancy, no one to help. I eventually had a C-section with the help of my neighbour, who was a nurse, and thankfully my baby and I survived. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every fortnight Sign up to Global Dispatch Get a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development team after newsletter promotion “In a normal circumstance, we would have known about this complication, but because there were no tests or medical professionals left in our town, not even an ultrasound machine, I had no way of diagnosing this,” she says. In another case, from earlier this year, Sergeevna says her colleagues were forced to treat a patient with endometriosis without anaesthesia. “She was bleeding when she came to the hospital. So there was no anaesthesia, not even power. And the nurse at the time used the torch on her phone to do the procedure because there was no other option.” View image in fullscreen A doctor holds up a baby born by caesarean section at Zaporizhzhia’s regional perinatal centre in May. Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP Accurate figures are not available; but organisations monitoring the situation in the region detect an anecdotal rise in maternal and child mortalities, as well as long-term health problems. There are also reports of difficulties in accessing contraceptives and abortion. From Ukraine and Sudan to Gaza: why have hospitals become a target of war? Read more Sergeevna says the situation is particularly acute for women, and that she had been dealing with women facing a range of mental health issues because of the lack of medical care and trauma they had suffered, including rape and sex slavery. She says one 18-year-old had come with the letter “Z” cut into her torso with a blade. While inspecting her wound, Sergeevna discovered the girl had been raped. “But that was not why she came to us; she was too ashamed to admit that. She came only because she couldn’t tolerate the wound any more because of swelling and inflammation.” With few doctors left in her district and depleting resources, Sergeevna and her team did their best to stitch her up. “But there was nothing else we could do for her. There were no resources to check her for STDs or provide her with contraceptives. We did not even have any way to provide psychological support.” * Name has been changed Explore more on these topics World news Ukraine in depth Ukraine Russia Maternal mortality Women's health Europe Infant and child mortality features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.dw.com/en/saudi-arabia-12-ki.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O76U Major airlines have suspended operations in Riyadh amid security threats [FILE: February 15, 2023] Image: Markus Mainka/picture alliance Advertisement At least 12 people were killed and hundreds were injured in an attack on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Saturday. "King Khalid International Airport was targeted by an attack, amid continued attacks targeting civilian aviation facilities in the kingdom," the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said in an initial statement. Hours later, the authority announced that 12 people had been killed, including four Saudis, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese national. At least 309 others were injured in the attack, the aviation authority said, adding that "all injured individuals are receiving the necessary medical care at several hospitals." Operations at the airport had been suspended until further notice. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen also announced that "a projectile" had also landed near King Fahd International Airport in the eastern city of Dammam. Coalition vows to respond On Sunday, the Saudi-led military coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government accused the Houthis of carrying out the deadly attack on Riyadh's international airport. The coalition vowed to respond "decisively." In a statement, coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki described the attack as a "war crime" and vowed the coalition "will respond decisively to this terrorist attack." Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump called the attack on Riyadh's international airport "not acceptable." He also told reporters that he will speak with Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. When asked if the US might get involved, Trump responded, "We'll find out." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio ‌said that ​the United States ​strongly condemns recent ​attacks ‌on ‌Saudi Arabia, confirming that ​an American citizen was killed ​in the strikes. "These reprehensible ⁠attacks ​demonstrate ​a blatant ​disregard for innocent ‌civilian life. ​They ⁠must stop now," ⁠Rubio ​wrote on X. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" by the Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport. "Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law," Guterres said. "These attacks must cease immediately." What do we know about the Riyadh attack? A Saudi official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told the Associated Press that many people were wounded after a missile hit a passenger terminal. The AFP news news agency also reported that a number of people were injured, citing a local medical source who also spoke on the condition of anonymity. "ER doctors are being called to hospitals across Riyadh," the source told AFP. "We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh." Ambulances were seen outside the passenger terminal Image: Social Media/REUTERS Several Western embassies in Riyadh, including those of Germany, the United States, Canada and Spain, urged citizens to avoid the airport. The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks" at the airport. Spain's embassy referred to a "new attack" by the Houthi rebels in Yemen while Canada's embassy warned of "ongoing military activity." What did the Houthis say? The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen did not immediately claim responsibility for the attack. However, after the attack, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree retweeted his own post from a day earlier in which he said that only pre-approved humanitarian flights would be allowed to land at Riyadh airport. In the retweet on Saturday night, Saree wrote: "A reminder." When asked about the attack, US President Donald Trump said the US would soon decide whether to join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen. "We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision," Trump told reporters at the White House. "We move very quickly." Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Strikes hit Riyadh airport earlier this week Fighting has intensified between Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government in Yemen. The Iran-backed Houthis have been launching strikes on targets in Saudi Arabia, including several this week on the airport in Riyadh that killed four people, injured several others, and damaged planes. Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways canceled multiple flights between their ​respective hubs and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday. Kuwait Airways also cancelled its flights on Saturday. King Khalid Airport was hit earlier this week in an attack claimed by Yemen-based Houthi rebels Image: Social Media/REUTERS Last month, Houthi rebels made advances on important strategic locations along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with a Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces seeking to take back those gains. The Houthis have responded by launching attacks into Saudi Arabia, which represents a significant escalation in their multi-year conflict with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government after a peace deal unraveled in July. The Saudi-backed government in Yemen last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, especially those around the Bab al-Mandab strait. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/15/russ.text: Russia detained a Swedish national and a Japanese journalist within days of one another as former president Dmitry Medvedev called on Moscow to replenish its "exchange pool" of Western citizens to trade for Russians held abroad.Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) said on Wednesday it arrested the Swedish citizen in the Sebezh district of Pskov region, near the borders with Belarus and Latvia.He is accused of entering Russia under cover of joining the Russian military while intending to carry out "sabotage and terrorist attacks" on military sites.The FSB said it established that from February to June the detainee served as commander of a drone section in the 24th separate assault battalion of Ukraine's Aidar unit — a volunteer formation that emerged during Russia's initial invasion of Ukraine in 2014 which the Kremlin has designated a "terrorist organisation," a common domestic classification aimed at Ukrainian units.He had allegedly admitted to serving in the unit. The FSB said it holds documents confirming his participation in combat against Russian forces, and that he faces charges of illegal border crossing, organising the activities of a terrorist organisation and serving as a mercenary. His name has not been disclosed.Sweden's government has not commented. Moscow's claims could not be independently verified.'You have to howl like a wolf'The second arrest — that of Yuki Imai, a journalist for Japan's Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper — took place on Sakhalin Island as he was preparing to leave the country, the FSB said.He is accused of gathering information on Russia's defence capabilities at the direction of Japanese intelligence services.Japan summoned Russia's ambassador in Tokyo Nikolai Nozdrev on Wednesday. Kimitake Nakamura, head of the foreign ministry's European affairs department, lodged a protest both over the arrest and Moscow's decision to announce it without first informing the Japanese government.Tokyo has demanded consular access to Imai and assurances of humane treatment.The Committee to Protect Journalists called for his immediate release, warning that journalists "must not be used as a bargaining chip in broader geopolitical disputes."The organisation estimates that at least 30 journalists are currently held in Russia in connection with their work.The arrests followed Medvedev's post on Telegram on 9 October calling for Russia to increase its "exchange pool" of foreign nationals it uses to negotiate the release of its citizens deemed useful to the regime.Writing after the arrest in Montenegro of Mikhail Zvinchuk, a Kremlin propagandist and founder of Rybar — a Telegram channel close to Russia's military and security services — Medvedev said Moscow might need to detain more Western nationals to secure the release of Russians held abroad."Now, quite likely, we will have to fill up the exchange pool with European and American idiots in order to pull our own people out," he wrote."There is no other way: if you live with wolves, you have to howl like a wolf." Zvinchuk has since been returned to Russia.Using people as bargaining chipsRussia has for years detained foreign nationals on charges including espionage and drug smuggling, a practice its critics describe as the taking of hostages for exchange.The most recent large-scale swap took place in August 2024, when 26 people were freed in a multinational exchange: Russia released 16 detainees, and Western countries handed back 10.Among those Russia released were Wall Street Journal journalist Evan Gershkovich, sentenced to 16 years in a high-security prison on espionage charges, and former US Marine Paul Whelan, convicted on the same charges and given the same sentence.Germany obtained the release of Rico Krieger, who had been sentenced to death in Belarus, and Patrick Schabel, detained at Moscow's Sheremetyevo airport over cannabis-infused gummy sweets.Russia received back, among others, Vadim Krasikov, who was serving a life sentence in Germany for the assassination of Georgian national Zelimkhan Khangoshvili in a Berlin park in 2019, Artem and Anna Dulcev, accused of spying in Slovenia under the guise of South American art dealers, and Pablo González aka Pavel Rubtsov, a Russian-born Spanish journalist who had been held in Poland on espionage charges since February 2022.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text: Mukhesh Ambani: the billionaire family’s conglomerate owns the Jamnagar refinery in Gujarat. Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPA View image in fullscreen Mukhesh Ambani: the billionaire family’s conglomerate owns the Jamnagar refinery in Gujarat. Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPA The age of extinction Earthshot prize Environmentalists criticise choice of Earthshot prize venue owned by fossil fuel firm Mumbai facility is part of Reliance Industries, owner of world’s biggest oil refinery and funder of controversial mega-zoo Supported by About this content Rebecca Ratcliffe , Gloria Dickie and Elisângela Mendonça Sun 8 Nov 2026 01.00 EST Last modified on Sun 8 Nov 2026 01.02 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Prince of Wales’s Earthshot prize will host its forthcoming annual awards ceremony at a venue owned by the billionaire Ambani family conglomerate, drawing criticism from conservationists over their fossil fuel businesses and their foundation’s controversial mega-zoo . A spokesperson for the Earthshot prize , which awards £1m to five winners every year to invest in conservation work, confirmed to the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay that this year’s ceremony will be held at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on 17 November. The venue is part of Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, which also owns Jamnagar, the world’s biggest oil refinery in Gujarat on India’s western coast. The group’s philanthropic arm funds the 400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo Vantara, which was founded by Mukesh’s son Anant Ambani and inaugurated by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, last year. The zoo is embroiled in a long-running controversy over its vast collection of more than 150,000 animals, which reportedly includes some of the world’s most endangered species – from the radiated tortoise, native to Madagascar, to the Spix’s macaw, endemic to north-eastern Brazil but now considered extinct in the wild . Megan Carr, of the Wildlife Animal Protection Forum South Africa (WAPFSA), warned that using a venue owned by Reliance “could lend an unearned environmental prestige to a corporate group currently under question by the global conservation community”. Conservation groups, including WAPFSA, have raised concerns about the speed with which Vantara has amassed so many animals, and about how they were sourced. The site, near the family’s oil refinery, houses more than 2,000 species of animals. This week, the 32-member committee that governs Cites, the UN-administered body that regulates trade in endangered species, requested that India submit another report on the steps it is taking to address concerns relating to its imports of protected species. The committee also requested the Cites secretariat review 11 cases where there are unresolved questions over how animals were sent to Vantara. Joanna Swift, the executive director of communications at the Earthshot prize, said it had not sought a philanthropic partnership for its award ceremony venue and that it was paying the standard commercial rate to rent the space. “The [Jio World Convention Centre] was selected because it allowed us to host the event in Mumbai while meeting the practical requirements of an event of this size. It offers world-class facilities, technical infrastructure and experience of hosting major international events, including environmental ones,” Swift said. “In February this year, JWCC hosted the first ever Mumbai climate week.” Vantara, Kensington Palace and JWCC have been approached for comment. Vantara has previously denied allegations of wildlife trafficking and says its purpose is “to rescue wild animals in distress, provide treatment along with lifelong care, and rehabilitate those fit for the wild”. “With regulatory approval, we also breed select endangered or extinct-in-the-wild species, serving as a modern Noah’s Ark to ensure their survival under human care and restore wild populations through reintroduction,” Vantara says on its website. Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo of allegations that animals had been acquired illegally or mistreated. A later Cites fact-finding mission raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential after newsletter promotion Susan Cheyne, the vice-chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s small apes section, said that Vantara’s model has not yet been shown to support conservation and “may be driving demand for wild animals in trade”. “For gibbons and other primates, this matters a great deal. Moving animals out of their range countries into a private facility does nothing for wild populations unless there is a transparent, credible plan for those animals: for welfare, for any conservation breeding with clear goals, and for return to range states where that is possible. Real rescue and sanctuary work for primates is done by underfunded centres in range countries,” Cheyne said. Daniela Freyer, co-founder of the German NGO Pro Wildlife, added: “Our planet is increasingly threatened by the overexploitation of wildlife and by climate change driven by fossil fuels. This week, the Cites Standing Committee, which oversees international wildlife trade, decided to keep India under its compliance procedure, as questions remain about the origin of some of the world’s rarest animals imported to Vantara. A prize whose goals include protecting nature and fixing our climate should be careful not to lend its reputation to these questions.” Vantara had sought to lobby the UK, the chair of this week’s Cites meetings, attempting to persuade officials to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara, the Guardian and Mongabay reported earlier this month. Ministers were advised not to engage formally with Vantara, internal documents revealed. The Earthshot prize, founded by Prince William in 2020, is billed as the most prestigious environmental award. William appeared on the BBC’s Graham Norton show last month to promote the prize, saying it was designed to “talk about urgency and optimism together”. Swift said that it was vital to host an edition of the Earthshot prize in India. “Mumbai is the sixth largest city on earth. It is home to exceptional environmental solutions and the people behind them, with an impact felt in India and around the world. Spotlighting progress like this, to the largest possible audience, is why the Earthshot prize exists,” Swift said.
